commands.example: `/desktop` opens the Desktop app and loads your current session. You can keep working from the richer interface.

commands.what: Toggle push-to-talk voice dictation. Hold Space to speak, release to send. Claude transcribes your speech into the input box.
commands.when: When typing is inconvenient — brainstorming ideas, dictating long descriptions, or working away from the keyboard.
commands.example: `/voice` enables voice mode. Hold Space, say 'add a login page with Google OAuth', release — your words appear as typed text.

commands.what: Cancel whatever Claude is currently doing — stop a generation, interrupt a command, or clear your current input. The universal 'stop' button.
commands.when: When Claude is going down the wrong path, a command is taking too long, or you changed your mind mid-generation.
commands.example: Claude starts editing the wrong file. Press Ctrl+C — it stops immediately. You can redirect it with new instructions.

commands.what: Exit Claude Code. Same as typing `/exit`. Sends an EOF (end of file) signal that closes the session gracefully.
commands.when: When you're done working and want to close the session. Faster than typing `/exit`.
commands.example: Press Ctrl+D — the session closes. Your conversation is saved and can be resumed with `claude -c`.

commands.what: Redraws the screen without clearing your conversation history. Fixes visual glitches or garbled output without losing anything.
commands.when: When the terminal display looks corrupted — overlapping text, broken borders, or visual artifacts after resizing.
commands.example: After resizing your terminal or tmux pane, the display looks wonky. Ctrl+L redraws everything cleanly.

commands.what: Toggle verbose output — shows detailed tool calls, MCP interactions, and behind-the-scenes activity. Like turning on subtitles for what Claude is doing.
commands.when: When you want to watch Claude work in real-time — seeing every file it reads, every search it runs, every tool it calls.
commands.example: Press Ctrl+O — now you see: 'Reading src/app.ts...', 'Searching for auth handler...', 'Editing line 42...'. Press again to turn it off.

commands.what: Opens interactive reverse search through your command history. Type to filter, press Ctrl+R again for older matches, Tab to accept, Ctrl+C to cancel.
commands.when: When you remember part of a previous prompt and want to find and reuse it without retyping.
commands.example: Press Ctrl+R, type 'glossary' — it finds your last prompt containing 'glossary'. Press Enter to use it, or Ctrl+R again to find an older one.

commands.what: Toggle the task list and tool trace visibility. Shows what tools Claude is calling and the progress of multi-step work.
commands.when: When you want to watch Claude's tool calls in real-time or check task progress during complex operations.
commands.example: Claude is working through multiple steps. Press Ctrl+T to see a live feed of tool calls and task checkboxes. Press again to hide it.

commands.what: Cycle through permission modes: default → acceptEdits → plan → auto. Controls how much freedom Claude has. Also available as Alt+M.
commands.when: When you want to quickly switch between giving Claude more autonomy (auto approves everything) or less (plan mode, read-only).
commands.example: Press Shift+Tab — the mode indicator at the bottom changes. Keep pressing to cycle: default (asks per tool) → acceptEdits (auto-approves file edits) → plan (read-only).

commands.what: Switch the AI model without leaving your current prompt. A quick toggle between models mid-thought.
commands.when: When you're about to ask something and realize you want a different model — faster or more capable.
commands.example: You're typing a complex question and want Opus instead of Sonnet. Press Option+P, select opus, continue typing.

commands.what: Toggle extended thinking mode. When enabled, Claude shows its reasoning process before answering — useful for understanding complex decisions.
commands.when: When you want to see how Claude is thinking through a problem, or when debugging why it made a particular choice.
commands.example: Press Option+T to enable. Ask a complex question — Claude first shows its reasoning steps, then gives the final answer.

commands.what: Toggle fast mode on/off with a keyboard shortcut. Same as `/fast` but without typing a command.
commands.when: Quick toggle when you want snappier responses for a few prompts, then switch back to normal mode.
commands.example: Press Option+O — fast mode activates (shown in the status bar). Press again to return to normal mode.

commands.what: Opens your current prompt in your default text editor (VS Code, vim, nano). Write a long, detailed prompt there with full editor features, then save and close to send it.
commands.when: When you need to write a complex, multi-paragraph prompt and the single-line input box feels too cramped. Also available as Ctrl+X Ctrl+E.
commands.example: Press Ctrl+G — your editor opens with your current text. Write a detailed feature spec, save, close — the text appears in Claude's input ready to send.

commands.what: Quick rewind — press Escape twice to open the rewind/checkpoint interface. Same as `/rewind` but faster.
commands.when: When Claude just did something wrong and you want to immediately undo back to a previous point.
commands.example: Claude edited the wrong file. Press Escape twice — the rewind interface appears. Select a checkpoint and everything rolls back.

commands.what: Navigate through your prompt history — previous messages you've sent in this session. Up goes to older prompts, Down goes to newer ones.
commands.when: When you want to reuse or modify a previous prompt. Faster than retyping.
commands.example: Press Up — your last prompt appears. Press Up again for the one before that. Edit if needed, then press Enter to send.

commands.what: Paste an image from your clipboard directly into Claude Code. Claude can see and analyze images — screenshots, diagrams, error messages, designs.
commands.when: When you want Claude to look at something visual — a screenshot of a bug, a design mockup, or an error dialog.
commands.example: Take a screenshot (Cmd+Shift+4 on Mac), then Ctrl+V in Claude Code — the image appears and Claude can describe and analyze it.

commands.what: Send running tasks or commands to the background. Important: in tmux (which you're almost always in), Ctrl+B is tmux's prefix key — so press Ctrl+B twice to send it to Claude Code.
commands.when: When a long-running task (build, test suite) is blocking the input and you want to keep talking to Claude while it runs.
commands.example: A test suite is running and blocking input. Press Ctrl+B Ctrl+B (double-tap because tmux) — it moves to the background. Keep working while it finishes.

commands.what: Bash mode — run a shell command directly from Claude's input and add its output to the conversation. The output becomes part of the context Claude can reference.
commands.when: When you want to run a terminal command and have Claude see the results — checking git status, running tests, or viewing logs.
commands.example: `! git status` runs git status and shows the output to both you and Claude. `! npm test` runs tests and Claude can help interpret the results.

commands.what: Trigger file path autocomplete. Type @ and start typing a filename — Claude Code suggests matching files from your project. Select one to reference it.
commands.when: When you want to point Claude to a specific file without typing the full path. Much faster and less error-prone.
commands.example: Type `look at @glo` — autocomplete suggests `src/data/glossary.json`. Select it and Claude reads that file.

commands.what: Add a comment that appears in the transcript but is NOT sent to Claude. Like a sticky note for yourself when reviewing the conversation later.
commands.when: When you want to annotate the conversation for your own reference without affecting Claude's behavior.
commands.example: `# this approach was suggested by Dong in the Lark chat` — visible in the transcript but Claude never sees it.

commands.what: Delete everything from the cursor to the end of the line. The deleted text is stored — paste it back with Ctrl+Y. Standard terminal text editing.
commands.when: When you want to quickly clear the end of your current input without backspacing character by character.
commands.example: You typed 'fix the login bug in the auth module' but want to change the ending. Put cursor after 'bug', press Ctrl+K — everything after 'bug' is deleted.

commands.what: Delete everything from the cursor to the start of the line. The deleted text is stored — paste it back with Ctrl+Y. Press repeatedly to clear multiline input.
commands.when: When you want to wipe your current input and start over, or clear a long prompt you've changed your mind about.
commands.example: You typed a long prompt but want to start over. Press Ctrl+U — the whole line is deleted. Much faster than holding backspace.

commands.what: Paste back text that was deleted with Ctrl+K or Ctrl+U. Like an undo for line deletions. Press Alt+Y after to cycle through older deletions.
commands.when: When you accidentally deleted text with Ctrl+K/U and want it back, or when you intentionally cut text to move it.
commands.example: You deleted a line with Ctrl+U, moved to a new position, then Ctrl+Y pastes it back. It's cut-and-paste for the terminal.

commands.what: Jump the cursor one word at a time. Alt+B moves backward (left), Alt+F moves forward (right). Much faster than arrowing one character at a time.
commands.when: When editing a long prompt and you need to jump to a specific word without holding the arrow key. On Mac, requires Option-as-Meta configured in terminal settings.
commands.example: Cursor is at the end of 'fix the login bug in auth'. Press Alt+B three times — cursor jumps back past 'auth', 'in', 'bug'. Edit from there.

commands.what: Start a new line in your prompt without sending it. Type a backslash then press Enter. Works in all terminals. Other options: Shift+Enter (iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty) or Option+Enter (Mac).
commands.when: When you want to write a multi-line prompt — listing requirements, writing detailed instructions, or pasting formatted text.
commands.example: Type `fix these issues:\` then Enter — a new line starts. Type `1. Login timeout\` Enter `2. Missing avatar` Enter. Send the whole multi-line message.

stack.what: A framework for building websites and web apps using React. Handles routing (pages), server-side rendering (fast page loads), and deployment optimization.
stack.why: Powers all our websites — HPM public site, KOT site, HPM internal app, and the home app. One framework, consistent skills across all projects.
stack.analogy: If building a website is like building a house, Next.js is the construction framework — it gives you the walls, plumbing, and wiring patterns so you can focus on the design.

stack.what: A system for styling websites using small, pre-made CSS classes directly in your HTML. Instead of writing separate style files, you add classes like `text-red-500` or `p-4`.
stack.why: Fast to build with, consistent across projects. When Claude writes `bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-lg`, that's Tailwind — blue background, white text, rounded corners.
stack.analogy: Like a LEGO set for design — snap together pre-made pieces instead of carving each one from scratch.

stack.what: An open-source tool that sits on top of your database and gives it a visual admin panel, user management, permissions, and an API — all without writing backend code.
stack.why: It's the operations backbone for HPM. Staff log in, manage projects, SOPs, and tasks through Directus instead of spreadsheets. 15 collections and counting.
stack.analogy: Think of it as a smart spreadsheet app that also handles user logins, permissions (who can see what), and connects directly to your website and apps.

stack.what: A powerful, reliable, open-source database. It's where all the actual data lives — Directus is just the interface on top of it.
stack.why: Industry standard, handles complex relationships well, scales as the business grows. Used by companies from startups to Instagram.
stack.analogy: If Directus is the filing cabinet's labels and drawer handles, PostgreSQL is the actual cabinet and the documents inside.

stack.what: A cloud platform for running servers and databases. You push code, Railway builds and runs it. Handles the infrastructure so you don't need to manage servers yourself.
stack.why: Hosts our Directus instance and PostgreSQL database. Easy to deploy, good logging, simple environment variable management.
stack.analogy: Like renting a fully managed office space — you bring your business (code), they handle the building, power, and security.

stack.what: A cloud platform specialized for frontend websites and apps. Automatically builds, deploys, and serves your site globally with excellent performance.
stack.why: Hosts all our Next.js sites (HPM, KOT, home app). Every push to GitHub triggers an automatic preview deploy. Production deploys go live globally in seconds.
stack.analogy: Like a worldwide chain of showrooms — your site is automatically replicated to servers near your visitors for the fastest possible load times.

stack.what: A platform for storing Git repositories in the cloud, collaborating through pull requests, and tracking issues. The social network for code.
stack.why: All HPM and KOT repos live on GitHub. It's where code review happens, PRs are opened, and the connection to Vercel auto-deploys from.
stack.analogy: Like Google Drive for code — but with built-in version history, collaboration tools, and the ability to track and discuss every change.

stack.what: An AI assistant that runs in your terminal and can read, write, and modify code, run commands, and help with development tasks interactively.
stack.why: Your primary development partner. Handles coding, debugging, deployment, and even building things like this glossary. Runs on the Mac Mini via SSH.
stack.analogy: Like having a developer sitting next to you who can read your entire codebase, answer questions, write code, and run commands — but in a chat window.

stack.what: A version of JavaScript that adds type checking — it catches certain kinds of bugs before the code even runs. Used in all our Next.js projects.
stack.why: Prevents common mistakes (like passing a number where text was expected). When a build fails with a 'type error', that's TypeScript doing its job.
stack.analogy: If JavaScript is writing a letter freehand, TypeScript is writing on a form — the form tells you exactly what goes in each field, catching mistakes early.

stack.what: A team messaging and collaboration platform (like Slack but popular in Asia). Supports webhooks for automated notifications.
stack.why: HPM/KOT team communication tool. Used for day-to-day chat and can receive automated alerts from our systems via webhooks.
stack.analogy: The team's digital office — chat rooms for each project, plus the ability for our tools to post automatic updates.

stack.what: A terminal multiplexer that keeps sessions alive in the background, lets you split screens into panes, and survives disconnects. The backbone of persistent remote work.
stack.why: Keeps Claude Code, dev servers, and logs running on the Mac Mini even when your laptop disconnects. Essential for SSH workflows — nothing dies when Wi-Fi drops.
stack.analogy: Like having a desk that stays exactly how you left it, even after you leave the building. Come back tomorrow, everything is still there — papers open, programs running.

stack.what: Anthropic's AI model and web platform (claude.ai). The intelligence behind Claude Code. Can also be used directly in the browser for research, writing, brainstorming, and analysis without touching code.
stack.why: The brain that powers the development workflow. Used via Claude Code in the terminal for coding, and via claude.ai in the browser for non-code tasks like writing specs, reviewing plans, and explaining concepts.
stack.analogy: If Claude Code is the developer sitting at the desk, Claude AI is the mind behind it — you can also talk to it directly in a browser for anything that doesn't need a terminal.

stack.what: Google's AI model and platform. Available via the web, Google Workspace integrations, and Gemini CLI. A capable alternative to Claude for research, code review, and second opinions.
stack.why: Used alongside Claude for cross-referencing, getting different perspectives on technical decisions, and tasks where Google ecosystem integration is useful (Docs, Sheets, Gmail).
stack.analogy: Like having a second advisor in the room — sometimes you want a different perspective before making a big decision. Claude and Gemini each have strengths.

safePractices.title: Always backup before changing the database
safePractices.rule: Export the Directus schema (collections, fields, relations, permissions) BEFORE and AFTER any migration or build that changes the database structure.
safePractices.why: If a migration goes wrong, you need a snapshot to restore from. The 'after' backup confirms what actually changed.
safePractices.how: Save to `backups/{buildname}_pre_{DDMMYY}/` before and `backups/{buildname}_post_{DDMMYY}/` after. Include a README with restore steps.
safePractices.realStory: This is a hard rule for all HPM/KOT builds. Even 'small' changes get backed up — because small changes have caused big problems before.

safePractices.title: Never commit secrets or credentials
safePractices.rule: API keys, database passwords, OAuth secrets, and any sensitive configuration go in environment variables (.env files), NEVER in the code itself.
safePractices.why: Once committed and pushed to GitHub, secrets are in the public history forever — even if you delete them in a later commit. Bots actively scan GitHub for exposed keys.
safePractices.how: Use `.env.local` for local development, set env vars in Railway/Vercel for production. Make sure `.env*` is in your `.gitignore` file.
safePractices.realStory: The HPM Google OAuth client_secret and Directus database URL are stored as environment variables on Railway. If they were in the code, anyone with GitHub access could see them.

safePractices.title: Check which branch you're on before working
safePractices.rule: Always run `git branch` or `git status` before making changes. Working on the wrong branch is one of the most common and frustrating mistakes.
safePractices.why: If you make changes on `main` instead of your feature branch, you might accidentally deploy unfinished work or create messy merge situations.
safePractices.how: Make it a habit: `git status` first thing. If you're on the wrong branch, `git checkout <correct-branch>` before touching any files.
safePractices.realStory: Imagine building a new KOT feature but accidentally doing it on the HPM branch. The HPM site deploys with random KOT code. Not fun.

safePractices.title: Use preview deploys before going to production
safePractices.rule: Always test on a preview/staging URL before deploying to production. Never push directly to the live site without testing.
safePractices.why: What works locally might break in production due to different environment variables, missing dependencies, or configuration differences.
safePractices.how: Push to a branch (not main) → Vercel creates a preview URL → test there → merge to main for production deploy.
safePractices.realStory: Every push to the KOT repo gets a preview URL. Kenny reviews changes there before we promote to the live kotprojects.com.

safePractices.title: Commit often with clear messages
safePractices.rule: Make small, focused commits with messages that explain what you did and why. Don't bundle 10 different changes into one giant commit.
safePractices.why: If something breaks, small commits make it easy to find and undo the exact change that caused the problem. Giant commits make debugging a nightmare.
safePractices.how: Commit after each logical piece of work. Message format: what you did + why. Example: 'Add artist bio field to support new profile layout'.
safePractices.realStory: Good: 3 commits for 3 features. Bad: 1 commit called 'various updates' with 47 file changes — good luck finding the bug.

safePractices.title: Pull before you push
safePractices.rule: Always pull the latest changes before pushing your own. This prevents merge conflicts and ensures you're working on top of the latest code.
safePractices.why: If someone else pushed changes and you push without pulling, your push will be rejected or create conflicts.
safePractices.how: `git pull` before `git push`. If there are conflicts, resolve them before pushing.
safePractices.realStory: If Claude pushed changes to the HPM repo overnight and you push without pulling, Git will reject your push. Pull first, resolve any conflicts, then push.

safePractices.title: Never use banned file name suffixes
safePractices.rule: Never name files with FINAL, FINAL_FINAL, NEW, or UPDATED. Use the versioning system: _v01, _v02, _WIP, _MASTER.
safePractices.why: Ambiguous names create chaos. 'FINAL_v2_NEW_UPDATED.pdf' tells you nothing. Version numbers and status suffixes are clear and sortable.
safePractices.realStory: This is the HPM/KOT naming standard. Claude flags non-conforming file names and renames them on the spot.

safePractices.title: Don't run destructive commands without thinking
safePractices.rule: Before running `rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git push --force`, or any command marked as dangerous — stop and ask: 'Can I undo this? Am I targeting the right thing?'
safePractices.why: These commands don't ask for confirmation and can't be undone. One wrong path in `rm -rf` can delete your entire project.
safePractices.how: Read the command twice. Check the target path. Ask Claude or a developer if you're unsure. There's usually a safer alternative.
safePractices.realStory: Claude Code itself follows this rule — before running any dangerous command, it asks for your permission first.

safePractices.title: Always name tmux sessions
safePractices.rule: When creating a tmux session, always use `tmux new -s <name>` with a descriptive name. Never create unnamed sessions.
safePractices.why: Unnamed sessions get numeric IDs (0, 1, 2) which are impossible to tell apart. After a few days, you'll have no idea which session holds what, and you'll waste time attaching to each one to check.
safePractices.how: Name after the project or task: `tmux new -s hpm-dev`, `tmux new -s kot-db-fix`. Use `tmux ls` to review what's running. Clean up stale sessions with `tmux kill-session -a`.
safePractices.realStory: Same philosophy as naming Claude Code sessions with `claude -n` — if you can't tell your sessions apart, you'll lose track of your work.

safePractices.title: Use 'attach -d' when switching devices
safePractices.rule: When reconnecting to a tmux session from a different device or screen size, use `tmux attach -d -t <name>` instead of plain `tmux attach`.
safePractices.why: tmux remembers the terminal dimensions of whatever was last attached. If you attached from a 27" monitor and now reconnect from a laptop, the panes stay sized for the big screen — everything looks squished with a band of dead space.
safePractices.how: The `-d` flag detaches the old viewport first, then attaches fresh with your current screen dimensions. Make it a habit whenever switching between your Mac Mini monitor and SSH from your laptop.
safePractices.realStory: This is one of the most common tmux frustrations for new users. The fix is simple but you have to know about the `-d` flag.

fileTypes.name: TypeScript
fileTypes.what: The main code files for our Next.js projects. `.ts` is pure logic, `.tsx` includes visual components (HTML-like elements).
fileTypes.you_see_it: Everywhere in the HPM, KOT, and home app projects. The files Claude edits most often.
fileTypes.note: Editing these without understanding can break the site. Leave to Claude or developers.

fileTypes.name: JavaScript
fileTypes.what: The original language of the web. Our projects mostly use TypeScript instead, but config files and some tools still use plain .js.
fileTypes.note: Config files are sensitive — small typos can break builds.

fileTypes.name: JSON data file
fileTypes.what: Structured data files. Used for configuration (package.json), data storage (this glossary!), and API responses.
fileTypes.can_edit: Carefully. JSON is strict — a missing comma or extra bracket breaks it. Use a JSON validator if editing manually.
fileTypes.note: package.json is especially important — it lists every package the project depends on.

fileTypes.name: Markdown
fileTypes.what: Text files with simple formatting (bold, lists, headers) that render nicely on GitHub. Used for documentation, specs, and plans.
fileTypes.you_see_it: README.md, CLAUDE.md, build specs, session logs, this glossary's source.
fileTypes.note: Safe to edit! Markdown is just formatted text. Use # for headers, - for bullets, **bold** for emphasis.

fileTypes.name: Environment file
fileTypes.what: Contains secret configuration — API keys, database URLs, passwords. NEVER commit these to Git.
fileTypes.you_see_it: At the root of projects. `.env.local` is for local development only.
fileTypes.can_edit: Yes, but carefully. Wrong values = broken connections. And NEVER push to GitHub.
fileTypes.note: If you see a .env file on GitHub, the secrets inside are compromised. Rotate them immediately.

fileTypes.name: Git ignore list
fileTypes.what: Tells Git which files to NOT track. Keeps secrets, build outputs, and system files out of the repository.
fileTypes.you_see_it: Root of every project. Lists patterns like `node_modules/`, `.env*`, `.DS_Store`.
fileTypes.note: Important for security. Make sure .env files and node_modules are always in here.

fileTypes.name: Stylesheet
fileTypes.what: Defines how things look — colors, spacing, fonts, layout. Our projects mostly use Tailwind instead of raw CSS.
fileTypes.you_see_it: Usually just `globals.css` in our projects, since Tailwind handles most styling inline.
fileTypes.note: Minor visual tweaks are possible, but Tailwind is preferred for consistency.

fileTypes.name: Project manifest
fileTypes.what: The ID card of a Node.js project. Lists the project name, all dependencies (packages it needs), and available commands (scripts).
fileTypes.you_see_it: Root of every project. This is what `npm install` reads to know what to download.
fileTypes.note: Managed by npm commands, not edited by hand. `npm install <package>` adds to it automatically.

fileTypes.name: Dependency lock file
fileTypes.what: An auto-generated file that records the exact version of every package installed. Ensures everyone working on the project gets identical dependencies.
fileTypes.you_see_it: Root of every project. Updated automatically by npm.
fileTypes.note: Never edit this manually. It's auto-generated. Always commit it to Git though — it ensures consistent builds.

symbols.name: Comments
symbols.what: Notes left by developers in the code that the computer ignores. `//` is a single-line comment, `/* */` wraps multiple lines.
symbols.example: `// TODO: add error handling` — a note reminding someone to come back and finish this part.

symbols.name: Arrow function
symbols.what: A shorthand way to write a function (a reusable piece of logic). The arrow says 'take this input and return this output'.
symbols.example: `const double = (x) => x * 2` — a function that takes a number and doubles it.

symbols.name: Code block / Object
symbols.what: Groups code together (like a paragraph) or defines structured data (key-value pairs). Context determines which.
symbols.example: In code: `if (loggedIn) { showDashboard() }` — run this if logged in. As data: `{ name: 'Dong', role: 'admin' }`.

symbols.name: Array
symbols.what: An ordered list of items. Can hold anything — text, numbers, objects, even other arrays.
symbols.example: `const artists = ['MA', 'ATS', 'TNY']` — a list of HPM artist codes.

symbols.name: Template literal
symbols.what: A special string that can include dynamic values using `${variable}`. More flexible than regular quotes.
symbols.example: `Hello, ${user.name}!` becomes `Hello, Dong!` — the variable is replaced with its actual value.

symbols.name: Variable / Shell prompt
symbols.what: In template literals: inserts a variable's value. In terminal: indicates the command prompt (where you type).
symbols.example: In code: `${artist.name}`. In terminal: `$ git status` means 'type git status at the prompt'.

symbols.name: Strict equality
symbols.what: Checks if two values are exactly the same — same value AND same type. `'5' === 5` is false (string vs number).
symbols.example: `if (user.role === 'admin')` — only true if the role is exactly the text 'admin', not a number or anything else.

symbols.name: Not equal
symbols.what: The opposite of equality checks. True when two values are different.
symbols.example: `if (status !== 'paid')` — do something if the status is anything other than 'paid'.

symbols.name: AND / OR operators
symbols.what: `&&` means both conditions must be true. `||` means at least one must be true.
symbols.example: `if (isAdmin && isLoggedIn)` — must be both. `if (isHPM || isKOT)` — either company works.

symbols.name: Spread operator
symbols.what: Expands an array or object into individual elements. Like unpacking a suitcase — takes everything out and lays it flat.
symbols.example: `const all = [...hpmArtists, ...kotClients]` — combines both lists into one.

symbols.name: Safe navigation
symbols.what: Safely accesses a property that might not exist. Instead of crashing, it returns undefined.
symbols.example: `user?.email` — get the email if user exists, otherwise just return undefined instead of crashing.

symbols.name: Default value
symbols.what: Provides a fallback value when something is null or undefined. 'Use this, or if it's missing, use that instead.'
symbols.example: `const name = user.name ?? 'Anonymous'` — use the user's name, but if it's missing, show 'Anonymous'.

symbols.name: Pipe / Union type
symbols.what: In the terminal: sends one command's output as input to another. In TypeScript: means 'this OR that type'.
symbols.example: Terminal: `git log | head -5` (show only first 5 log entries). TypeScript: `type Status = 'draft' | 'published'` (can only be one of these).

symbols.name: Type annotation
symbols.what: Declares what type of data a variable holds. Helps catch bugs before the code runs.
symbols.example: `const projectName: string = 'HPM'` — this variable must always be text, never a number.

symbols.name: Asynchronous code
symbols.what: Handles operations that take time (fetching data, reading files) without freezing the app. `await` pauses until the result arrives.
symbols.example: `const artists = await directus.items('artists').readByQuery({})` — wait for Directus to return the artist data before continuing.

faqs.question: Why can't I see the dev server from my laptop?
faqs.answer: The dev server runs on the Mac Mini at `localhost:3000`, but 'localhost' means 'this machine'. Your laptop is a different machine. You need an SSH tunnel to bridge them.
faqs.solution: Use `ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 mini` from your laptop. This makes the Mac Mini's port 3000 appear as your laptop's port 3000. Then open localhost:3000 in your laptop's browser.

faqs.question: Why did the Vercel deploy fail?
faqs.answer: Vercel runs `npm run build` on their servers. If it fails, it's usually a code error (TypeScript type errors, missing imports) or a missing environment variable.
faqs.solution: 1. Check the Vercel build logs for the specific error. 2. Run `npm run build` locally to reproduce it. 3. If it's an env var issue, check Vercel project settings → Environment Variables. 4. Fix the error, commit, and push — Vercel will auto-retry.

faqs.question: Why can't staff log in with Google?
faqs.answer: Directus Google OAuth has specific requirements: the user must exist in Directus with provider set to 'google', their email must be in GCP's test user list (while in testing mode), and all the environment variables must be exactly right.
faqs.solution: Check: 1. User exists in Directus with correct email and provider='google'. 2. Email is in GCP console → OAuth consent screen → Test users. 3. All AUTH_GOOGLE_* env vars are set on Railway. 4. PUBLIC_URL matches the actual Railway URL exactly.

faqs.question: What's the difference between Vercel and Railway?
faqs.answer: Vercel is for frontend/websites (Next.js sites that visitors see). Railway is for backend/servers (Directus and the database that stores data). They serve different purposes and work together.
faqs.solution: Think of it as: Vercel = the storefront (what customers see), Railway = the back office (where data lives and is managed). The storefront calls the back office's API to get the data it needs.

faqs.question: I changed something but the site looks the same?
faqs.answer: Could be caching (browser or Vercel showing an old version), deploying to preview instead of production, or the change is on a branch that hasn't been merged to main yet.
faqs.solution: 1. Hard refresh the browser (Cmd+Shift+R). 2. Check which branch the change is on (`git branch`). 3. Check if Vercel deployed the latest commit (Vercel dashboard). 4. If preview, the live site won't change until you merge to main.

faqs.question: What does 'merge conflict' mean and what do I do?
faqs.answer: Two branches changed the same part of the same file. Git doesn't know which version to keep, so it asks you to choose. This is normal — not an error.
faqs.solution: Don't panic. Git marks the conflicting sections in the file. You (or Claude) need to edit the file to pick the right version, remove the conflict markers, then commit. Ask Claude for help if unsure — resolving conflicts is a routine part of development.

faqs.question: Why does Claude ask for permission before some commands?
faqs.answer: Claude Code has a safety system. Safe commands (reading files, checking status) run automatically. Dangerous or irreversible commands (deleting, force-pushing, modifying production) require your explicit approval.
faqs.solution: Read what Claude is asking to do. If it makes sense, approve it. If you're not sure, ask Claude to explain what the command does and whether it's reversible. This is a feature, not a limitation — it prevents accidents.

faqs.question: Why do we backup Directus schema before AND after changes?
faqs.answer: The 'before' backup is your safety net — if the migration breaks something, you can restore the previous state. The 'after' backup records what the migration actually did, serving as documentation.
faqs.solution: This is a non-negotiable rule for all HPM/KOT builds. Claude handles this automatically. Pre-backup goes to `backups/{buildname}_pre_{DDMMYY}/`, post-backup to `backups/{buildname}_post_{DDMMYY}/`.

faqs.question: What's a branch vs a fork vs a worktree?
faqs.answer: Branch: a parallel line of work within the same repo (most common, used daily). Fork: a complete copy of someone else's repo under your account (for contributing to external projects). Worktree: multiple branches checked out in separate folders simultaneously (for working on two things at once without switching).
faqs.solution: For day-to-day HPM/KOT work, you'll almost always use branches. Forks are for external open-source code. Worktrees are for when Claude needs to work on two features simultaneously.

faqs.question: What does 'type error' mean in the build?
faqs.answer: TypeScript found a mismatch — like trying to use a number where text was expected, or accessing a property that doesn't exist. It's catching a potential bug before it reaches users.
faqs.solution: Read the error message — it tells you the file, line number, and what it expected vs what it got. Claude can fix most type errors automatically. Think of it as spell-check but for code logic.

faqs.question: Why is my terminal session gone after I close my laptop?
faqs.answer: A regular terminal session is tied to your connection. When the connection closes (laptop lid, Wi-Fi drop, SSH timeout), the terminal and everything running inside it dies. tmux prevents this by running sessions in the background, independent of your connection.
faqs.solution: Always work inside tmux. Start with `tmux new -s dev` (or whatever name fits). If you get disconnected, reconnect with `tmux attach -t dev` — everything is exactly where you left it. The processes never stopped.

faqs.question: Why does my tmux look weird or squished on a different screen?
faqs.answer: tmux locks its display to the smallest attached viewport. If you were on a big monitor and now connect from a small laptop screen (or vice versa), the panes stay sized for the old screen — leaving dead space or squishing everything.
faqs.solution: Use `tmux attach -d -t <name>` instead of plain `tmux attach`. The `-d` flag detaches the old viewport first, then attaches fresh with your current screen dimensions. This instantly fixes the sizing.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a tmux session and a Claude Code conversation?
faqs.answer: They solve different problems. A tmux session keeps your terminal processes alive — dev servers, logs, running commands. If tmux dies, those processes die, but your code files are safe on disk. A Claude Code conversation preserves your AI chat context — what you discussed, what Claude knows about your task. Claude saves conversations to disk (~/.claude/), so even if tmux crashes, the conversation history survives. Think of tmux as the room you work in (keeps the lights on) and Claude Code as the notebook on the desk (keeps your notes safe even if the room loses power).
faqs.solution: Use both together: tmux keeps your workspace alive across disconnects, and Claude Code's `-r` or `-c` flags let you resume conversations. If tmux crashes, `claude -r` recovers the conversation. If Claude crashes, tmux keeps your other panes (dev server, logs) running.

troubleshooting.problem: Site shows 'Cannot connect' or 'This site can't be reached' in browser
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Dev server isn't running, wrong port, or no SSH tunnel
steps: Check if the dev server is running (look for 'ready on localhost:3000' in the terminal)
If working from laptop → Mac Mini: make sure you used `ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 mini`
Try opening the URL in an incognito/private window (clears browser cache)
Check if another process is using the same port: `lsof -i :3000`

troubleshooting.likely_cause: Code error, missing environment variable, or dependency issue
steps: Go to Vercel dashboard → select project → Deployments → click the failed deploy
Read the build log — the error is usually near the bottom
Common fix: run `npm run build` locally to see the same error
If it mentions an env var: check Vercel → Project Settings → Environment Variables
Fix the issue, commit, push — Vercel auto-retries

troubleshooting.problem: Google login shows 'Access denied' or '403' on Directus
troubleshooting.likely_cause: User not in GCP test users, provider not set, or env var mismatch
steps: Check GCP Console → APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen → Test users — email must be listed
Check Directus → Users — user must exist with provider='google'
Verify Railway env vars: AUTH_GOOGLE_* vars, PUBLIC_URL must match exactly
Clear cookies and try again — stale session tokens cause weird errors
Check if GCP consent screen is still in 'Testing' mode (limits to listed test users only)

troubleshooting.likely_cause: Insufficient file permissions or trying to edit a protected file
steps: Check if you're in the right directory and logged into the right machine
For SSH config files: you may need to edit from the machine directly, not over SSH
For npm: try `sudo npm install` only as a last resort (and only if you understand why)
For Git: check if you have push access to the repo on GitHub

troubleshooting.problem: 'Module not found' or 'Cannot find module' error
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Missing package dependency or wrong import path
steps: Run `npm install` — the package might not be installed locally
Check if the import path is correct (typos, wrong folder, missing file extension)
Check `package.json` — is the package listed in dependencies?
If it was recently added by someone else: `git pull` then `npm install`

troubleshooting.problem: Changes committed to the wrong branch
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Forgot to check/switch branch before making changes
steps: Don't panic — Git tracks everything
If not pushed yet: `git log` to see the commit, then ask Claude to help move it to the right branch
Prevention: always run `git status` before starting work to see which branch you're on
Claude will typically check this for you, but it's a good habit to develop

troubleshooting.problem: Directus collections or fields not showing up after migration
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Cache, browser session, or migration didn't fully complete
steps: Hard refresh Directus (Cmd+Shift+R)
Log out and log back in (session might have stale permissions)
Check Railway logs for migration errors
Compare against the post-migration backup to verify the schema matches expectations

troubleshooting.problem: Git says 'rejected' when trying to push
troubleshooting.likely_cause: Remote has commits you don't have locally — someone (or another session) pushed first
steps: Run `git pull` to get the remote changes first
If there are merge conflicts: resolve them (or ask Claude to help)
After resolving: commit the merge, then push again
NEVER use `git push --force` to override this — it destroys the other commits
